name: James' Court
description: James' Court was built from 1727 by James Brownhill, from whom it takes its name, and quickly became one of Edinburgh's most fashionable addresses - philosopher David Hume lived here before moving to the New Town, and diarist James Boswell later took over Hume's old flat. The buildings behind Gladstone's Land, some dating to the 16th century, still convey the crowded feel of the 18th-century Old Town.
interesting_fact: James Boswell entertained Samuel Johnson here during Johnson's 1773 visit to Edinburgh, the very trip that produced Johnson's 'A Journey to the Western Islands of Scotland'.

name: The Jolly Judge
description: Tucked below street level just off the Lawnmarket, the Jolly Judge is a traditional basement pub known for its low beamed ceilings and roaring log fire - a world away from the busier tourist bars further down the Royal Mile. Its location close to the Sheriff Court and High Court once made it a favourite haunt of the city's legal community.
interesting_fact: In 2024 the Jolly Judge was named CAMRA Edinburgh Pub of the Year and also picked up Cider Pub of the Year, recognition for a pub that deliberately keeps the music off to stay a genuinely quiet place to drink.

name: Susannah Alice Stephen Memorial
description: This memorial seat, topped with a bronze sculpture of a parakeet and garden trug by sculptor Frances Pelly, sits in James' Court in honour of Susannah Alice Stephen (1960-1997), a landscape designer who co-founded the Scottish Society of Garden Designers before her death in a diving accident off the Galapagos Islands. She chose this spot deliberately, knowing that pioneering town planner Patrick Geddes - a hero of hers for bringing green space into Edinburgh's Old Town - had once lived in James' Court himself.
interesting_fact: The memorial is inscribed with the line 'Keep your face towards the sun and the shadows will fall behind you', a fitting motto for a landscape designer who spent her career finding light and green space within the dense, shadowed closes of the Old Town.
source_notes: Ad hoc backlog batch 2026-09-02. Located within James' Court itself, not near Makars' Court as initially assumed from photo sequence order - corrected via research confirming its actual location.

name: The Ensign Ewart
description: This Lawnmarket pub, trading in some form since at least 1680, was renamed in 1938 in honour of Ensign Charles Ewart of the Royal Scots Greys, who captured the eagle standard of the French 45th Regiment of the Line at the Battle of Waterloo in 1815. The name was chosen the same year Ewart's remains were reburied with full honours at Edinburgh Castle.
interesting_fact: A large painting of the Battle of Waterloo hangs inside, alongside Scottish military memorabilia - the pub sits only a few hundred metres from Ewart's actual grave on the Castle esplanade.
source_notes: Ad hoc backlog batch 2026-09-02. Distinct from the existing 'Ensign Ewart Memorial and Grave' POI (leg 8, Castle Esplanade) - this covers the pub itself, further down the Lawnmarket.

name: Boswell's Court
description: Boswell's Court on Castlehill dates from the 17th century and takes its name not from the famous diarist James Boswell but from his uncle, Dr John Boswell, a physician who lived here. James did visit his uncle at this address in October 1762, and a plaque on the building - now home to the Witchery restaurant - also claims that James Boswell and Samuel Johnson dined here around 1770.
interesting_fact: The stair entrance still carries a carved lintel bearing a merchant's mark and the initials 'T' and 'L', thought to belong to an earlier owner, Thomas Lowthian.

name: Ramsay Lane
description: Ramsay Lane climbs steeply from the Royal Mile up toward the Castle esplanade, named for the poet Allan Ramsay, whose distinctive octagonal house - nicknamed 'the goose-pie house' for its unusual shape - once stood at its head. The lane connects Castlehill to Ramsay Garden, the striking Arts and Crafts tenement development built around Ramsay's old home in the 1890s.
interesting_fact: Ramsay Garden was one of the first projects of town planner Patrick Geddes, who saw restoring housing on the Castle slopes as a way to bring the professional classes back to live in the Old Town.
